name: user_settings
description: Per-member settings that only the member themself reads. Same shape as settings, different lifecycle: millions of rows instead of dozens, loaded with the session instead of at startup, and never polled.

columns.name: user_id
columns.description: Leading column of the primary key, so one range scan returns everything the session needs.

columns.name: key
columns.description: A key from ../user_settings.json. Same grammar and the same stability rule as settings.key.

columns.name: value
columns.description: Same text form and same parse rule as settings.value: the registry declares the type, the column carries the decimal string, 'true'/'false' or UTC milliseconds. A key whose type is uint64 and whose meaning is a row elsewhere carries that id as a decimal string — see main_creation_group — with no foreign key behind it, so an id that resolves to nothing is read as unset.
columns.note: NULL is an explicit null where the registry allows one. An absent row is the unset case.

notes: One query per session, never a join per row. The session loads a member's settings once when it is built and holds them; a request that renders another member never reads this table. That is the whole reason the table can exist without costing anything.

Which flags may move here, and which may not, is decided by the query and not by the topic: a flag that appears in a WHERE, JOIN or ORDER BY over many users stays a column on users. hide_amount_gdd and hide_amount_gdt are only ever read for the logged-in member (legacy backend/src/graphql/model/User.ts), so they move. gms_allowed does not: legacy filters on it in backend/src/apis/gms/ExportUsers.ts, and as a key that export becomes a join per row. avatar_visible_to_members is read when showing a profile to someone else and stays a column for the same reason.

The columns moving off users: hide_amount_gdd, hide_amount_gdt, their defaults there are the legacy column defaults — false, false — because anything else changes a migrated member's behavior silently. main_creation_group joins them from the other side: it replaces the user_creation_groups table rather than a column, for the reason ../user_settings.json gives.

Rows may be deleted here; deleting one restores the registry default. Unlike settings there is no cross-instance marker to keep honest, because these are own writes: the member changes their own setting in the request whose session holds it. Another instance holding a session for the same member learns nothing — which is the same staleness the session model already accepts everywhere else.
Deletion of the row is not tied to deletion of the member. users.deleted_at is a soft delete, so nothing here is removed when a member leaves.

No index beyond the primary key. Its leading column is user_id, which serves the only query this table has. A lookup of one key across all members is not a query the product makes; if it ever becomes one, the index belongs here before it is written.
Timestamps are UTC milliseconds; see types/Timestamp.json.
Identifiers are uint64 throughout; see contracts/AGENTS.md.
